Bert Shaw, Arthur Allum and Jack Flower were all running strongly and we rejoiced to find our ninth man in front of Birchfield's sixth. Over the last lap many places were gained, our Taylor-Shields-Carter trio, in particular, pegging back many opponents.
Patience, Jack Flower and H. Shields are well up with the leaders, and a good finish is already assured.
Carter leads Footer by a yard at the top of Copse Hill, and they stride up the steep incline like two horses, with no sign of fatigue. Then come Jack Flower, Shields, Allum, Ring D.
Jack Flower, taking the seventh stage, regained the lead for us and gave Shaw a useful lead which Footer and Allum slightly increased, to win a new record time.
Jack Flower was our next baton carrier, and started off with the breath of the Birchfield man, J.
The 2 Miles was easily the most exciting race of the evening. Tom Carter, Jack Flower and Syd Ring were running for us and they had G.

In the 1 Mile we did rather better and with Harry Shields second and Jack Flower third, we managed to level matters somewhat. The 880 yards saw Jim Tosh turning out once again and he ran in quite his old form in winning in 2 min. 4 3-5 secs.

With Jack Flower fourth, we thus had an easy win, with, as mentioned above, Ashcombe finishing second and Thames Valley H. third. We now had a 4 points lead and, barring accidents, the Shield looked as good as won.
Alec Patience once again dropped us to fourth place, but Syd Ring brought us up one, and then Jack Flower gave us the lead for the first time.
In the next relay of about 4¾ miles, Jack Webster came in for Birchfield; and showing some of his old form, he ran splendidly in putting his team 28 seconds in front of Jack Flower at the take-over.

The 2 Miles team race was an easy win for our boys, Tom Carter leading Art. Penny and Jack Flower home. The 1 Mile Medley Relay saw Michael run a fine half-mile stage to give us a lead that was kept throughout.
Allum, Patience brothers, Jack Flower and Ted Stimpson, who was unfortunate enough to have trouble with his leg, which forced him to retire.

Herbert continued his good running by winning with Syd Ring and Jack Flower in the next two positions. Scoring 12 aside, the points were—Belgrave H. 151, R.N. & R.M. 274, Met.
The first Club championship for the "Griffin" Cup was held, and won by Jack Flower in 15 min. 21 sec. Duffett was second, and Micky Pyer third.
Footer, who also won the handicap with a 10 seconds allowance. Jack Flower and Arthur Allum took the place medals. Footer won the Surrey County Championship and also led our team to an easy win.

Jack Flower.—Belated news that he is in Iraq and is sporting " one Pip and a Sam Browne." From Exeter.—News has just reached us that Doubleday (" Doub ") is safe and returning to London as soon as possible.
Lieutenant Jack Flower, in the Middle East, sends his best wishes " To all my friends in the best Club in England." (How's that you fellahs!)

Bill Snell, in the M.E., says he and "Charlie Churcher seem to be chasing one another but never meeting. But one fine morning saw Jack Flower, complete in claret and gold, trying out his spikes in the sand.

When cycling through Balham, he tried a hand-spring on the handlebars, but landed in the road on his neck—which he gave a crick! However, a week's rest in hospital, with the sister of Joe and Jack Flower to hold his hand, soon put him right again.
Bill still sees Capt.
Jack Flower is now home and out of the Army. Has put on a lot of weight, a fact readily believed by those who have seen him.
The 1932 race also found the club finishing too far back, their position being 10th. Jack Flower and Bert Footer both ran well and our scoring six were: J.
The 100 yards boys' race saw Ken Eales score an easy win and it was interesting to see the sons of Jack and Joe Flower, two old club champions, competing in this event.

Jack Flower (4th stage) had a three seconds lead over the Poly when handing over and 2 min. 2 sec. lead over Birchfield. Arthur Penny ran our fifth leg and finished 61 sec. ahead of the Poly with Birchfield nearly three minutes away; we were well on our way to our first victory!
The winner on this occasion-Les Cohen, followed by Footer, Jack Flower, Duffett, Penny, Allum, Rice, Pyer, with, needless to say, a Belgrave team win of convincing proportions.
Close behind were Jack Flower 15th, and Tom Carter 16th; Alf Taylor 27th, completed our scoring team, passing man after man including team-mates, in the last half mile.

It was with sadness that we received the recent news of JACK FLOWER's death at his home in Ruislip. Jack was one of our prominent runners in the 1930's and figures in many of our winning and placed teams as we climbed the ladder of fame.

ALBERT MACHER, JACK MACHER and JACK FLOWER were collectively in our thoughts during that minute of remembrance; and sharing that moment too was JACK HARTLEY of Coventry Godiva, guest at our last dinner in his capacity as ECCU President, and whose loss is mourned by the Midland club and its neighbours.

Highgate and South London were overtaken by Belgrave’s Jack Flower by the time the race reached Mitcham but Jack was, in turn, passed by the international Jack Holden, who had taken Tipton’s colours to the front.
